title: The integrated project management plan
blurb: Know what goes into an integrated project management plan (why, what, how, who, when, how much) and what an effective format looks like.
question: A housing association has approved the business case to refurbish 200 occupied flats. The sponsor asks the newly appointed project manager to 'produce the plan' before any work starts. What should an integrated project management plan contain, and what format makes it effective?

teach.h: One plan that holds all the plans
teach.body: The integrated project management plan (PMP) brings all of a project's subsidiary plans and management approaches together into one coherent, agreed document. It sets out why the project is being done, what it will deliver, how, by whom, when and for how much. In plain English: it is the project's single rulebook and route map. The project manager produces it (in a linear life cycle, mainly during Definition), the sponsor approves it, and it then becomes the baseline for delivery.

teach.caption: These six answers are the backbone. The management approaches below explain how the project will be controlled.

teach.h: The management approaches it pulls in

children.label: Control
children.sub: Risk and issue, change and configuration, quality

children.label: Delivery
children.sub: Procurement, health and safety, sustainability, transition

teach.caption: Each approach may be a short section or a separate subsidiary plan referenced from the PMP. What matters is that they all agree with each other.

teach.body: An effective PMP is clearly structured, so each reader can find the section they need. It is version-controlled: one current issue with a change history. It is approved by the sponsor, and owned and maintained by the project manager. It should also be proportionate: a two-month office move needs a few pages, a new hospital far more. Once approved it is the baseline, and it changes only through change control, so everyone works from the same version.

steps.label: Definition

steps.label: Deployment
steps.sub: Used to monitor and control; updated via change control

teach.h: The PMP in linear and iterative life cycles
teach.caption: Both still need the management approaches: risk, quality, communication, transition and so on.

teach.body: Riverside Homes is refurbishing 200 occupied flats. Its PMP links to the business case (lower energy bills, decent homes standard), defines the scope (windows, boilers, kitchens; lifts excluded) and success criteria, and explains the linear approach with a quality inspection per flat. A RACI names the sponsor, PM, contractor and resident liaison officer. It sets a block-by-block schedule and a budget with contingency, and covers risk, change, resident communication, procurement, safety in occupied homes, waste recycling and handover to maintenance.

teach.text: Classic confusions: the PMP is NOT just the Gantt chart (that is only the 'when'), and it is NOT the business case (the 'why', owned by the sponsor). The project manager owns and maintains the PMP; the sponsor approves it. An option saying the sponsor writes the PMP, or that it is frozen once signed, is wrong.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name each content item and add its purpose in one clause, e.g. 'Schedule: shows when key deliverables and milestones fall.'
Spread your points across why, what, how, who, when and how much, rather than five kinds of cost.
Include at least one management approach (risk, change, quality, communication), not only baselines.
If asked about format: clearly structured, version-controlled, approved by the sponsor, owned by the PM.
Anchor each point in the scenario, naming its deliverables and stakeholders.
The PMP integrates all subsidiary plans and approaches into one coherent, agreed document.
It answers why, what, how, who, when and how much, plus risk, change, quality, communication, procurement, safety, sustainability and transition.
Format: clearly structured, version-controlled, approved by the sponsor, owned and maintained by the PM.
Linear: a detailed baseline written in Definition. Iterative: written in Foundations, fixing time and cost with prioritised scope.
Once approved it is the baseline and changes only through change control.

summary: You can now list the typical contents of an integrated project management plan under why, what, how, who, when and how much, plus the management approaches it draws in. You can also describe an effective format and say who owns and approves the plan in linear and iterative projects.

A.q: Which document brings all of a project's subsidiary plans and management approaches together into one coherent, agreed whole?
A.why: The integrated PMP draws the subsidiary plans and approaches into one agreed document covering why, what, how, who, when and how much.

whyNot.0: The business case justifies the project (the why). It does not set out how all the plans fit together.
whyNot.2: The WBS breaks the work into packages. It feeds the scope and schedule sections but is only one part of the plan.
whyNot.3: A benefits management plan covers how benefits will be tracked and realised: one input, not the integrating document.

A.q: Who normally owns and maintains the integrated project management plan?
A.why: The project manager produces, owns and maintains the PMP day to day. The sponsor approves it.

whyNot.0: The sponsor approves the PMP and owns the business case, but does not maintain the plan.
whyNot.1: The steering group gives direction and decides at gates; it does not maintain the PMP.
whyNot.3: A project office may support planning with templates and tools, but ownership stays with the PM.

A.q: Which of the following would you NOT expect to find in an integrated project management plan?
A.why: Timesheets record work already done and are data used for monitoring. They are not part of the plan itself.

whyNot.1: How risks will be identified, analysed and managed is a standard PMP section.
whyNot.2: The schedule and milestones answer the 'when' question.
whyNot.3: The communication and stakeholder engagement approach is a typical PMP section.

B.q: On a hospital IT upgrade, the project manager presents a detailed Gantt chart to the board and calls it 'the plan'. What is the main weakness?
options: Gantt charts cannot show any milestones
The sponsor should have drawn the chart
A plan is only needed once work begins
It shows when, but not why, who or how
B.why: A Gantt chart covers the 'when'. An integrated PMP also explains why, what, how, who and how much, plus the approaches to risk, change, quality and communication.

whyNot.0: Gantt charts routinely show milestones, often as diamonds.
whyNot.1: The PM, not the sponsor, normally builds the schedule and the PMP.
whyNot.2: The PMP is produced before deployment so it can be approved as the baseline.

B.q: Complete the statement: an effective PMP is clearly structured, ______, approved by the sponsor, and owned and maintained by the project manager.
B.why: Version control means one current issue with a change history, so everyone works from the same plan.

whyNot.1: The PMP communicates the approach to stakeholders, so it should be accessible, not hidden.
whyNot.2: It is a living document, updated through change control rather than frozen.
whyNot.3: The PM writes and maintains it; the sponsor approves it.

B.q: An insurer is building a claims app using an iterative life cycle. How will its PMP differ most from one for a linear project?
options: It will have no risk or quality sections
Every feature is specified before work starts
Scope flexes, while time and cost are fixed
It is written by the product owner alone
B.why: An iterative PMP (written in Foundations) fixes time and cost and sets out high-level, prioritised scope, with detail planned time box by time box.

whyNot.0: Iterative projects still need risk, quality, communication and other management approaches.
whyNot.1: Specifying every feature up front is the linear way; in iterative projects scope emerges and is prioritised.
whyNot.3: The product owner prioritises the backlog, but the PMP is still produced and maintained by the project manager.

C.q: Which THREE would you expect in the PMP for a new rail depot? (1) the procurement approach (2) the transition approach (3) the health and safety approach (4) each engineer's appraisal rating
C.why: Procurement, transition, and health and safety approaches are all typical PMP sections. Appraisal ratings are line-management records, not plan content.

whyNot.0: Item 4 is wrong: individual appraisal ratings are HR records, not project plan content.
whyNot.2: Item 4 is wrong, and item 1 (the procurement approach) is missing.
whyNot.3: Item 4 is wrong, and item 2 (the transition approach) is missing.

C.q: A project manager emails slightly different versions of the PMP to the sponsor, the contractor and the team. Which feature of an effective PMP is missing?
options: A tailored plan for every audience
C.why: Version control ensures there is one approved, current PMP, so everyone works to the same baseline.

whyNot.0: The PM owns the PMP; the sponsor approves it. Sponsor ownership would not fix conflicting versions.
whyNot.1: More cost detail would not stop people working from different versions.
whyNot.2: Different plans for different people is the problem here. Communications can be tailored; the plan itself must be one agreed version.

C.q: On a two-year ERP project, the sponsor asks why the PMP needs a transition section when handover is 18 months away. What is the best answer?
options: Handover and readiness need planning from the outset
The PMP must be formally re-approved at transition
The sponsor is no longer accountable after handover
Transition costs always sit outside the project budget
C.why: Transition should be planned from the outset: user training, support arrangements and business readiness take time to arrange, and the PMP is where that approach is agreed.

whyNot.1: Gates do review the plan, but that is not why transition must be planned early.
whyNot.2: The sponsor remains accountable for benefits after handover.
whyNot.3: Transition activities and their costs are part of the project and its budget.

reteach.title: Think of it as the wedding planning folder
reteach.question: A couple planning a wedding keep a guest list, a budget spreadsheet, a timetable for the day and the caterer's contract. What turns these into one integrated plan?

blocks.body: On their own, the guest list, budget, timetable and supplier contracts are just lists. The wedding plan works when they are pulled together and checked against each other: 120 guests means the caterer quotes for 120, the venue holds 120 and the budget covers 120 meals. The couple (the sponsors) approve it; the wedding planner (the PM) keeps it current. Change one part and the others are updated too.

head: Wedding folder
PMP equivalent
rows: Budget plus a 'just in case' pot

blocks.text: A timetable on its own is not the wedding plan, just as a Gantt chart is not the PMP. Integration means every part agrees with every other part, in one current version.

explain.body: The opening sections say why the project exists (its objectives and link to the business case) and what it will deliver: scope, deliverables, exclusions and the success criteria used to judge it. Writing down exclusions prevents scope arguments later.

test.q: Which part of a PMP states what the project will and will not deliver?
test.why: The scope section defines the deliverables and, just as importantly, the exclusions.

whyNot.0: The communication approach says how and when stakeholders will be informed.
whyNot.1: The risk management approach says how risks will be identified and managed.
whyNot.3: A resource histogram shows resource demand over time.

explain.body: The 'how' covers the life cycle, methods and quality approach. The 'who' covers the organisation: roles, the organisational breakdown structure (OBS), resources and a RACI chart showing who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for each work package.

test.q: In a PMP, where would you show that exactly one person is accountable for each work package?
test.why: A RACI chart maps the OBS against the WBS and shows exactly one Accountable person per work package.

whyNot.0: A Gantt chart shows timing, not accountability.
whyNot.2: An S-curve shows cumulative cost or progress over time.
whyNot.3: The risk register names risk owners, not work-package accountability.

explain.body: The schedule sets out activities, milestones and key dates. The budget turns the estimates into a time-phased budget, plus contingency for known risks. The two must match: if the schedule moves, the spending profile moves too.

explain.caption: The schedule is the 'when'; costing each bar over time gives the 'how much'.

test.q: Which pair of contents answers the 'how much' question in a PMP?
test.why: The budget (built from the estimates) and the contingency held for known risks answer 'how much'.

whyNot.0: Milestones and float belong to the schedule: the 'when'.

explain.body: Clearly structured, version-controlled, approved by the sponsor, owned and maintained by the project manager. After approval it is the baseline; it changes only through change control so there is always one current version.

test.q: Which statement about the integrated PMP is correct?
options: The PM owns it and the sponsor approves it
The sponsor owns it and the PM approves it
The PMO owns it and the board approves it
The team owns it and the users approve it
test.why: The project manager owns and maintains the PMP; the sponsor approves it.

whyNot.1: This reverses the roles: the sponsor approves, the PM owns.
whyNot.2: A PMO may support the PM, but does not own the plan.
whyNot.3: Team members contribute estimates and detail, but the PM owns the plan and the sponsor approves it.
